narrative:
The model estimates there’s an 11 % chance you won’t pass your final year, which is just above the 10 % threshold that triggers the requirement to take extra help. This doesn’t mean you’re certain to fail, but it does mean the school wants to give you additional support now so you can finish strong.

Three things stood out when the model looked at your situation. First, you’ve never failed a class before, and that actually works in your favor—it’s the single biggest reason the model thinks you can still succeed. Second, you’ve said you want to go on to higher education, and that ambition also pushes the prediction toward passing. On the other hand, the model noticed you spend less than two hours a week studying outside of class, which is below what most of your classmates report. That limited study time is the main factor nudging the prediction toward a higher risk of failing.

Other details paint a mixed picture. Your parents both have higher education and your family relationships are very good, which are positive signs. However, you don’t have internet at home, and your free time after school is much lower than average, which might make it harder to catch up on your own. The school’s decision to require extra courses is really about giving you more structured time to study and ask questions before the final exams. If you use these sessions to build a regular study habit, you can bring that risk back down and keep your plans for higher education on track.
